items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Charlie Johnson, for one that had the orchestra at the Smalls’ Paradise... I was asked to join them, which I did.

ctx.x: Going back to your own development as a professional musician around this time, and now we’re in the mid-twenties, I guess, you began to work with some of the name orchestras in Harlem.

Yes. Well, let’s see, who were they? Charlie Johnson, for one that had the orchestra at the Smalls’ Paradise. Prior to that I played with the sextet of June Clark, who was at Small’s smaller place. When Edwin Smalls opened his Smalls’ Paradise over on Seventh Avenue, then he put in the big band, Charles Johnson, and I was asked to join them, which I did. That was a nice gig; we enjoyed it; had a lot of fun, a lot of fun guys. Charlie himself was a delightful man to work with, and to work for, I might add.
Billy Paige’s orchestra, that was earlier for you.

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: I started arranging when I was with Charlie Johnson's orchestra at the Small's Paradise.

ctx.x: Now when did the arranging come in, and let's bring that up to 1928, sort of, or up to the point where you joined Fletcher Henderson.

Actually, I started arranging when I was with Charlie Johnson's orchestra at the Small's Paradise. I started arranging by writing saxophone choruses, you know, for 3 saxophones, because that's what we had then, and there were 3 saxophones -- Benny Whittet, Benny Waters and Benny Carter. Three Bennys in the saxophone section.

And I used to write the saxophone choruses, you know, the rhythm section, because they knew all the chord changes and I knew the chord changes, but I didn't know how to do anything else. And I decided I wanted to arrange. I started studying what they called 'stock arrangements' -- arrangements by Don Redman, Archie Blyer, Arthur Lang, Walter Paul; I guess, Jimmy Dale, Jack Mason ... these are the names I remember, and I used to layout the parts on the floor and study them. And I started arranging just like that;…

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: Well, you know, people often say on the basis of your recordings, that one of your earliest bands that you played with was Charlie Johnsons. Yes.

ctx.x: Well, it depends upon how you would define genuinely ... certainly it is not synonymous with complete. But you know, I was learning. I was still, of course, undergoing the learning process, which even at this point, I still am -- but that was pretty early.
Well, you know, people often say on the basis of your recordings, that one of your earliest bands that you played with was Charlie Johnsons.
